body.heading: Full, but not full
paragraphs: Imagine a hotel with infinitely many rooms, numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on forever - and every single room occupied. A new guest arrives at reception. In any ordinary hotel, this is a short conversation. Here, the manager simply asks every guest to move to the room with the next number up: the guest in room 1 moves to room 2, room 2 to room 3, and so on. Every guest still has a room - and room 1 is now free.

This is Hilbert's hotel, a thought experiment popularised by the mathematician David Hilbert in the 1920s. It is not a trick about hotels; it is a precise demonstration that infinity does not behave like a very large number. 'All rooms taken' and 'room available' can both be true when the hotel never ends.

body.heading: An infinite bus arrives
paragraphs: Now a bus arrives carrying infinitely many new guests, numbered by their seats. Can the hotel cope? Yes: ask every current guest to move from room n to room 2n. All the even rooms are now filled and all the odd rooms - infinitely many of them - stand empty for the bus passengers. The hotel absorbed infinity into infinity and still had infinitely much room to spare.

And there is a deeper surprise waiting beyond the hotel. The mathematician Georg Cantor showed that some infinities are genuinely bigger than others: the counting numbers can be listed forever, but the real numbers cannot be listed at all - any attempt leaves some out. Infinity comes in sizes, and Hilbert's hotel is the friendly front door to that strange landscape.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Test the manager's method with a finite model: take rooms 1 to 10, all full, and try the 'move up one' trick - it fails at the top room, which shows exactly why the hotel must be infinite for the trick to work. Infinity is not a big number; it is the absence of a top room.

Then take the classic challenge: infinitely many buses arrive, each carrying infinitely many guests. Can the hotel fit them all? It can - one classic solution assigns rooms using prime numbers. Sketching even a rough version of that scheme is a genuine taste of research-level thinking.

takeaway: Infinity plus one is still infinity: in Hilbert's hotel, 'full' and 'room available' can both be true, because infinite sets can match up one-to-one with a part of themselves.
